content: In Greek mythology, ichor is described as the ethereal substance that flows as the blood of the gods. It is sometimes said to be present in ambrosia or nectar, the divine sustenance of the gods. When a god was injured and bled, the ichor in their blood rendered it toxic to mortals, emphasizing its otherworldly and dangerous nature. The term ichor has also been used in vampire lore to describe the blood within a vampire's veins. While many vampire stories and films depict their blood as reddish or dark red, others portray it as fundamentally different from human blood, often described as a dark green ichor, further emphasizing their supernatural essence. H.P. Lovecraft frequently employed the term ichor in his descriptions of alien or otherworldly creatures. One notable example is in his story The Dunwich Horror, where he vividly describes the grotesque remains of Wilbur Whateley, incorporating ichor to heighten the sense of the unnatural and horrific. In modern fantasy literature, the term ichor is often misused by authors seeking an alternative word for blood or ooze. This overuse has led to its becoming a cliché in some contexts. Ursula Le Guin, in her essay From Elfland to Poughkeepsie, critiques this misuse, calling the term the infallible touchstone of the seventh-rate, highlighting its overuse in subpar fantasy writing. In science fiction, ichor has been used as a substitute for alien blood. For instance, in Garth Nix's book Shade's Children, ichor is employed to describe the blood of extraterrestrial beings. Similarly, in Anne McCaffrey's Dragonriders of Pern series, the term is used to refer to the blood of the genetically engineered Pernese dragons, which are alien in origin but modified by humans.
